In multi-core multi-mode VCOs, transformer-based resonant tanks are preferred for their design ﬂexibility and area efﬁciency. However, as the number of operation modes increases, transformer design becomes challenging and the coupling network becomes complex, both of which tend to introduce asymmetries across VCO cores. As a result, the asymmetry induced by transformers or even other components inevitably introduces frequency mismatches in multi-core operation, which theoretically degrade the PN performance. Therefore, a fully symmetrical architecture in multi-core multimode VCOs are preferred to eliminate the negative impact on the PN performance.

A substantial number of state-of-the-art triple-mode orquad-mode VCOs have been proposed in recent years. A dualcore triple-mode VCO with a wide FTR of 80.6% and a PN of −137.9 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset from 7.15 GHz is proposed by using Electrical-Magnetic (E-M) mixed coupling in [15]. However, the asymmetrical inductance seen from each core causes inter-core mismatches that degrades the PN. Moreover, the inclusion of additional mode switches and switched capacitor arrays (SCAs) impose extra parasitics, thus reducing the FTR. A quad-core quad-mode VCO in [22] achieves an FTR of 101% and a PN of −133.2 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset from 13.7 GHz by using E-M mixed coupling, whereas the issue of asymmetrical inductance persists, and the parasitics from electric coupling capacitors negatively impact the FTR. Additionally, the non-uniformity of the FTR across each mode is also undesirable. With the same total FTR, a uniform FTR

in each mode yields roughly equal overlaps between adjacent modes, as shown in Fig. 1(a). In contrast, a nonuniform FTR makes the overlaps highly uneven, as shown in Fig. 1(b). This gives rise to two concerns. First, large differences in overlap make the band-decision thresholds difﬁcult to unify and require additional algorithm adaptation, which increases system complexity. Second, under PVT variations, the smaller overlap is more likely to shrink and create a frequency gap between adjacent modes. Other works still suffer from these issues [18], [21]. In summary, although multi-core multimode VCOs have demonstrated superior performance in terms of FTR and PN, issues such as asymmetrical inductance, parasitic-induced FTR reduction, and nonuniform FTR still persist, ultimately degrading the overall performance of the VCOs.

To surmount these issues, this work proposes a quadcore quad-mode VCO that achieves ultra-wide bandwidth and low PN by employing MR technique and fully symmetric architecture, which effectively eliminates the asymmetry and extra parasitics, and ensures a uniform FTR across all modes. This article is organized as follows. Section II presents the structure of the proposed VCO and the operating principles of the four modes. Section III discusses the symmetry of the design and its optimization of performance. Section IV presents the measurement results and Section V draws the conclusion.

subsections.title: Proposed VCO Design
paragraphs: quad-mode VCO, which consists of four identical single-core

VCOs, an embedded switched inductor (Lsw) and a modeswitching (SW) array. The active cores (Core-1, -2, -3, and -4), each composed of cross-coupled transistors, a tail resistor array, a pair of varactors and 6-bit SCA, are identical. The tail resistor array, shown in the bottom-left of Fig. 13(a), consists of a bypass path and a 13-bit programmable resistor bank. It is added to tune the core transconductance Gm versus frequency so that the excess loop gain G X = Gm RT (with RT the tank’s equivalent parallel resistance) remains moderate, which in turn limits ﬂicker noise up-conversion [26]. The 6bit SCA, shown in the top-left of Fig. 13(a), and the MOS varactors provide coarse tuning and continuous ﬁne tuning, respectively. The varactor is implemented using a thick-oxide device, with dimensions of W/L = 32/0.4 \mum. As the bias increases from 0 to 2.5 V, the varactor capacitance decreases from 35.7 to 15.2 fF (C = 20.5 fF) with Q larger than 29. The SCA exhibits an LSB of 7.7 fF, thereby enabling ﬁne and continuous frequency tuning. With a high Cmax/Cmin ratio preserved and Q kept moderate, the total capacitance ranges from 191.9 to 732.1 fF, and Q remains above 24 at 10 GHz. Each core is connected to its respective inductor ports in a center-symmetric manner, ensuring uniform coupling and balanced performance across all modes.

Furthermore, to maintain uniform capacitive loading at eachport, the SW array is designed with four identical sub-arrays, all positioned at the center of the transformer symmetrically. Each sub-array contains four switches and there are a total of sixteen switches in all. An additional switch is positioned along the routing of the switched inductor to control its on/off state. As discussed above, eight switches need to be turned on and another eight switches need to be turned off in each mode. The switch on-off states in each mode are shown in Fig. 13(b). sections.title: MEASUREMENT RESULTS
paragraphs: The proposed quad-core quad-mode VCO is implementedin 65 nm bulk CMOS with a core chip area of 0.152 mm2, as shown in Fig. 21. Fig. 22 shows the measured PN at 4.28, 8.66, 11.57, and 15.07 GHz, respectively, from four distinct modes. The measured FTR is 113.2% (4.21–15.18 GHz), with the frequency in each mode ranging from 4.21 to 6.24 GHz, 5.62 to 8.66 GHz, 7.52 to 11.6 GHz, and 10.01 to 15.18 GHz, respectively, as shown in Fig. 23. In each mode, the tuning voltage ranges from 0 to 2.5 V. It’s worth noting that the minimum frequency overlap between two adjacent modes is 10.5%, which further validates the robustness of the wide bandwidth. We further report the VCO gain KVCO on this plot at Vtune = 1.2 V . Fig. 24(a) and (b) show the measured PN, FoM and FoMT over the whole FTR, respectively, where the PN is from −108.8 to −120.3 dBc/Hz and −130.7 to −141.4 dBc/Hz at 1 and 10 MHz offsets while the FoM and FoMT vary from 180.0 to 190.5 dBc/Hz and 201.1 to 211.6 dBc/Hz at a 10 MHz offset.

The tank’s effective parallel resistance RT varies by mode, owing to variations in Q across modes. Since mode-1 exhibits the largest Q and thus the largest RT , it requires the smallest gm and hence the lowest current consumption, while the higher frequency and lower Q modes require more. In the proposed design, a programmable tail resistor array is used to adjust the current. In mode-1, a larger tail resistor is used to moderate gm, while smaller resistors are employed in modes-2 and -4 to allow higher gm. The VCO consumes 1.44 to 14.12 mW power under a VDD of 0.4 V, with mode-1: 1.44–3.27 mW; mode-2: 9.51–13.46 mW; mode-3: 11.14–14.10 mW; and mode-4: 12.63–14.12 mW. Although the 0.4 V low supply voltage helps reduce intrinsic power consumption of the VCO, an on-chip regulator is typically required to suppress noise and improve the power supply rejection ratio (PSRR), which results in additional power overhead. Across different modes, the Kpush of the proposed VCO is measured to range from 126 to 297 MHz/V. Since spur level depends on the PSRR, an on-chip regulator with high PSRR is required to keep spurs low. Although magnetic coupling brings Q variations, the tail resistor array ensures the robust start-up and also suppresses ﬂicker noise up-conversion across a wide FTR. This effect is reﬂected in the 1/f3 PN corners in each mode, which span 35–220 kHz (mode-1), 130– 210 kHz (mode-2), 180–600 kHz (mode-3), and 90–750 kHz (mode-4). A lower corner frequency indicates more effective suppression of ﬂicker noise up-conversion. Thanks to the tail resistor, the normalized PN (to 1 GHz) shows good ﬂatness with minimal variations across the whole FTR, as shown in Fig. 24(a). Moreover, Fig. 25 shows that the proposed VCO exhibits the best overall performance in view of FoM and FTR, and the best FoMTA in similar operating frequencies. The results are compared with state-of-the-art wideband VCOs in Table I, where the proposed VCO exhibits the largest FTR and the largest FTR overlap facilitated by MR technique, validating the robustness of the ultra-wide bandwidth.
